title: At the Mouth of the River
setting: Singapore and the Johor Sultanate, January-February 1819
description: You are a junior interpreter with Raffles' expedition. The East India Company wants a port near the Straits, but Dutch power and a disputed Johor throne make every word risky. Listen to key figures, inspect notes, and advise what kind of agreement should be made at Singapore.
learningObjectives: Explain why the East India Company wanted a port at the Straits.
Describe the disputed Johor succession in 1819.

player.name: Junior Interpreter
player.role: Junior interpreter attached to Raffles' expedition
player.brief: You translate, compare claims, and report what each leader seems to want.

sharedContext.text: In early 1819, Raffles is looking for a British trading post near the Straits. He needs a safe harbour for trade, but he must avoid a clash with the Dutch. Singapore seems promising, yet only the Sultan can grant land lawfully, and the Johor throne is disputed. As a junior interpreter, you must hear each side and help shape the next step.

spans.quote: British merchants trading with China complained that they had no safe harbour of their own at the southern end of the Straits of Malacca.
His instructions were cautious: he was to establish a post at the southern end of the Straits but to avoid any collision with the Dutch
only the Sultan of Johor could lawfully grant land to the Company.
And the Johor throne itself was disputed.

endings.title: A Treaty Is Signed
endings.summary: Raffles proceeds with Hussein and the Temenggong. The British gain their new trading post at Singapore.

historicalOutcome.text: This matches the record. On 6 February 1819 the treaty was signed by the Company, Hussein, and the Temenggong. The Dutch protested, but the dispute was settled in 1824 when they withdrew their objection to the British presence.

spans.quote: On 6 February 1819 a treaty was signed between the East India Company, represented by Raffles, Sultan Hussein and Temenggong Abdul Rahman.
The Dutch protested at once.
The dispute was finally settled by the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824, in which the Dutch withdrew their objection to the British presence in Singapore.

historicalOutcome.text: In the record, Raffles did not delay. Hussein arrived in early February 1819, Raffles recognised him, and a treaty was signed on 6 February. The British then kept their foothold despite Dutch protest.
